newsitem.title: USA: Patients not told when they used as guinea pig - paper.
newsitem.headline: Patients not told when they used as guinea pig - paper.

text.p: Patients are not always fully informed that they are guinea pigs in medical research studies authorized by the U.S. Food & Drug Administration, a newspaper said Sunday.

The Plain Dealer newspaper said it analyzed FDA files obtained under the Freedom of Information Act and found that in 4,154 inspections of researchers testing new drugs on humans, the FDA cited more than 53 percent for failing to fully disclose the experimental nature of their work.
"The risks, alternatives or uncertainties were obscured or incompletely explained," the newspaper said.
"Asked about the FDA's inspection reports, Mary Pendergast, the FDA's associate commissioner, said she considered them 'representatitve of biomedical research as a whole'," the paper said.

Government agencies and industry spend at least $20 billion a year on clinical trials, involving hundreds of thousands of people, to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of new treatments, the paper said.
"Many experiments do occur with appropriate safeguards," it said, adding nearly half of all inspected research is conducted without deficiencies in informed consent.

In one 1980-1982 study at a Miami, Fla., hospital, 500 people, some as young as 15, were injected with radioactive dye without their permission, which the FDA's Pendergast termed a "company-to-researcher miscommunication," the paper said. A researcher said he knew of no one harmed, it said.

In another case, the paper said it identified a 64-year-old woman, listed by a code name in FDA files, who died in 1988 in a Philadelphia hospital after being given an experimental gallstone treatment involving infusion of a solvent also used as a gasoline additive.
Her family said they had been unaware the treatment was experimental, it said.
The Plain Dealer said it identified her by matching information on her death certificate with the FDA files.
The FDA halted experimental use of methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE) the following year, the paper said. Nine of 29 patients had suffered "adverse effects" to infusions, the paper said.
The doctor involved in the research told the paper he had obtained consent from every patient and did not believe MTBE caused any harmful side effects, the paper said.

The paper said its overall analysis of FDA files was "strikingly similar to what a White House advisory committee discovered in 1995 when it examined patient-consent documents from more than 100 ongoing government research projects."
Last month, it said, the FDA relaxed informed-consent rules to allow experimental drugs in emergencies.
